To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) salt intake affects blood pressure in rats and in man, (2) in rats the effect is linear, (3) in humans the effect may be non-linear, (4) the slope is much steeper in salt-sensitive individuals.
the salt balance is a homeostatic system that can be disturbed in two opposite ways: (a) too little salt in the diet, and (b) too much salt in the diet.

the "salt balance" is a highly sensitive and important regulator of the blood pressure, but that this balance can be shifted to a "high setpoint" by a genetic predisposition to hypertension, which is not necessarily linked to salt sensitivity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of salt homeostasis, and the effects of salt intake on blood pressure and other cardiovascular risk factors, in rats and man.
the mechanisms of salt and blood pressure homeostatic regulation, and the role of salt for hypertension in man, with particular reference to salt-sensitive individuals.
the physiological aspects of salt balance, including the mechanisms involved.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the importance of salt intake in relation to hypertension is still not well understood.

salt is not the only, nor the main, cause of essential hypertension; that it is a factor of some importance, especially when other risk factors are at hand, and that it is a risk factor of some importance in the minority of salt sensitive subjects.
salt is a risk factor for hypertension, but not the cause".
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
salt intake is of little importance for blood pressure in most individuals, but may be of considerable importance for a few, especially when other risk factors are at hand.
, though salt intake may not be the only factor in hypertension, it may still be of major importance in the development of the disease.

, in spite of the great importance of salt for life in general, its role for blood pressure is not so simple, and that the salt intake of the great majority of people in the Western World is not the main culprit for the high prevalence of hypertension.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in the absence of other predisposing factors, salt sensitivity is a rare phenomenon, and that the vast majority of mankind is salt resistant, and can be expected to tolerate a rather wide range of intales.
the physiological salt setpoints are not far apart in rats and men, and that the majority of mankind can tolerate a wide range of salt intakes without any significant effects on blood pressure.

the salt balance of a population, and of the individual, should always be considered in relation to the total intake, and that this should be considered in relation also to the intake of other nutrients and to the metabolic rate of the individual.
